title: How Your Nose Smells the World
summary: How tiny smell receptors inside your nose catch floating molecules, send signals to the brain, team up with taste, and why some smells suddenly bring back old memories.
poll: Smell is the sense most closely linked to memory.

versions.title: How Your Nose Smells
versions.text:
Smell a flower. Smell bread. How does your nose know what it is?

Your nose is on your face. Air goes in and out when you breathe.

High up in your nose is a tiny spot. It is full of tiny parts. You have lots of them.

The air has tiny bits in it. You can not see them. They float into your nose.

Each tiny part is like a lock. Only some bits fit it. It is like a key in a lock.

When a bit fits, the part sends a signal. The signal goes to your brain.

Your nose and your tongue work as a team. Your tongue tastes a few things. Your nose adds most of the taste.

That is why food tastes dull when your nose is blocked.

A smell can wake up a memory. It can make you think of a happy day, fast.

versions.title: How Your Nose Smells
versions.text:
Smell a flower, then smell some bread. How does your nose know what each one is?

Your nose sits on your face. Air flows in and out of it when you breathe.

High up in your nose is a small spot. It is full of tiny parts, and you have lots of them.

The air around you has tiny bits in it. They float all around, even though you cannot see them. They go into your nose when you smell something.

Each tiny part is shaped a bit like a lock. Only some bits fit it, just like one key fits one lock. When a bit fits, the part sends a signal.

That signal goes fast to your brain. Your brain then tells you what you are smelling.

Your nose and your tongue work together as a team. Your tongue can only taste a few things, like sweet and salty. Your nose adds most of the taste to food.

That is why food can taste dull when your nose is blocked by a cold.

A smell can also wake up an old memory fast. One sniff can make you think of a happy day from long ago.

versions.title: How Your Nose Smells the World
versions.text:
Smell a flower, then smell a loaf of warm bread. You can tell at once which is which. How does your nose sort out so many smells so fast?

Your nose sits on your face. Air flows in and out of it each time you breathe, even when you do not notice.

High up inside your nose is a small patch of tissue called the olfactory epithelium. It is packed with tiny cells called receptors, and each type can catch one kind of smell.

The air around you is full of tiny floating bits called molecules. Every smell, from flowers to bread, is really a cloud of molecules drifting through the air and landing inside your nose.

Each receptor is shaped like a tiny lock. Only molecules of a certain shape fit a certain receptor, much like one key fits one lock. When a matching molecule fits, the receptor fires off a signal.

That signal races along a nerve into the brain, which sorts the signals before naming the smell.

Your nose and your tongue work closely as a team. Your tongue alone can only detect a handful of basic things, such as sweet, salty, sour, bitter, and umami. Most of what people call flavor comes from smell.

That is why food tastes dull and plain when a cold blocks the nose, since the tongue is left working almost alone.

Smell signals also travel fast into brain areas tied to memory and emotion, more directly than other senses do. That is why a smell, like a certain soap, can bring back a strong memory.

versions.text:
Smell a flower, then smell a loaf of warm bread baking in the oven. In an instant, you can distinguish which is which, even with your eyes shut tight. How does your nose manage to sort through so many different smells so quickly and so accurately?

Your nose sits at the front of your face, and air flows in and out of it every single time you breathe, whether or not you ever consciously notice the process occurring.

High up inside your nasal cavity is a small patch of tissue called the olfactory epithelium. It is packed with millions of specialized sensory cells called receptors, and each distinct type of receptor is built to recognize one particular kind of molecule.

The air around you is constantly full of tiny floating particles called molecules. Every smell, from flowers to fresh bread, is really a cloud of molecules drifting through the air and dissolving onto the moist tissue lining the nose.

Each receptor is shaped somewhat like a highly specific lock. Only molecules of a certain shape fit a given receptor, much like one key fits one particular lock and absolutely no other. When a matching molecule fits snugly into place, the receptor fires off an electrical signal that carries precise information about that particular molecule. A smell must also reach a certain threshold of strength before a receptor will respond to it at all.

That signal travels along the olfactory nerve into a region of the brain called the olfactory bulb, which sorts, strengthens, and combines the incoming signals before relaying a processed pattern deeper into the brain, where it is finally recognized as a particular, familiar smell.

Your nose and your tongue work closely together as a team. The tongue alone can only detect a small handful of basic tastes, including sweet, salty, sour, bitter, and umami. Most of what people casually call flavor actually comes from smell molecules rising up the back of the throat from food while it is being chewed and swallowed.

That is precisely why food tastes dull and oddly plain whenever a cold blocks the nose, since the tongue is then left working almost entirely on its own, without any contribution from smell.

Unusually, smell signals also travel directly into brain regions tied closely to memory and emotion, more directly than signals from most other senses manage to do. That is why one familiar smell, such as a certain soap or a certain spice, can suddenly evoke a strong, vivid memory from long ago, even one a person had almost completely forgotten about.

questions.stem: Where are smell receptors located, according to the article?
options: On the surface of the tongue's taste buds
In a patch of tissue high inside the nose
Deep inside the stomach, near food
On the outside surface of the face
questions.why: The article says receptors sit in a patch of tissue called the olfactory epithelium, high up inside the nose.

wrong.A: Taste buds on the tongue detect taste, not smell.
wrong.C: The stomach is not mentioned in the article.
wrong.D: Receptors are inside the nose, not on its outer surface.

questions.stem: What does the article say the olfactory bulb does to incoming signals?
options: It sorts and strengthens the signals
It erases signals that are too strong
It sends signals straight to the tongue
It stores signals as permanent memories
questions.why: The article says the olfactory bulb sorts the signals before they are named.

wrong.B: The article never says signals are erased.
wrong.C: Signals go deeper into the brain, not to the tongue.
wrong.D: Memory storage is linked to other brain areas, not described as the bulb's job.

questions.stem: In the article, what does the word detect mean when it describes the tongue?
options: To build something new
To forget something quickly
To combine two different foods
To notice or sense something
questions.why: The article uses detect to mean sensing or noticing a taste.

wrong.A: Detecting is not about building anything.
wrong.B: Detecting is the opposite of forgetting.
wrong.C: Combining foods is a separate idea from detecting a taste.

questions.stem: Why does the author compare a molecule fitting a receptor to a key fitting a lock?
options: To explain how real locks and keys are made
To describe what molecules are made of
To show that only a matching shape triggers a signal
To argue that smell is not very useful
questions.why: The lock-and-key comparison helps readers picture why a receptor only responds to a matching molecule shape.

wrong.A: The article is not about how real locks are made.
wrong.B: Molecule composition is not explained through this comparison.
wrong.D: The article treats smell as very useful, connecting it to flavor and memory.

questions.stem: What happens when a cold blocks the nose, based on the article?
options: The tongue works alone, so food tastes dull
The brain stops sending any signals at all
Receptors multiply to replace the blocked ones
The olfactory bulb grows larger than before
questions.why: The article says that when a cold blocks the nose, the tongue is left working almost entirely alone, so food tastes dull.

wrong.B: The brain keeps working on whatever signals it receives.
wrong.C: The article does not mention receptors multiplying.
wrong.D: The article does not say the bulb changes size from a cold.

questions.stem: Zaid smells his uncle's cologne and suddenly feels happy, remembering a wedding. What explains this best?
options: Cologne always smells the same to every person
The tongue stores emotional memories like this
Only unpleasant smells can bring back feelings
Smell signals travel directly to memory and emotion areas
questions.why: The article says smell signals travel into brain areas tied to memory and emotion more directly than other senses, which explains Zaid's reaction.

wrong.A: How cologne smells to everyone is not the point of this example.
wrong.B: The tongue is not described as storing memories.
wrong.C: The article does not limit this effect to unpleasant smells.

questions.stem: Based on the article, why might flavor depend on more than the tongue alone?
options: Because the tongue can detect thousands of smells by itself
Because the nose and tongue combine signals to create flavor
Because flavor depends only on how food looks
Because the stomach decides what flavor food has
questions.why: The article explains that most of flavor comes from the nose working together with the tongue.

wrong.A: The article says the tongue alone detects only a handful of basic tastes.
wrong.C: Appearance is not discussed as part of flavor in the article.
wrong.D: The stomach is not mentioned in relation to flavor.

MID.prompt: Explain how smell and taste combine to create flavor, and describe one way smell connects to memory or emotion. Use at least three ideas from the article.
checklist: I explained how the nose and tongue combine to create flavor.
I described one connection between smell and memory or emotion.
I used at least two key words, such as receptor, molecule, or detect.
MID.modelAnswer: Receptors in the nose detect tiny floating molecules and send signals to the brain, while the tongue only detects a few basic tastes like sweet and sour. These two signals combine to create what we call flavor, which is why food tastes dull when a cold blocks the nose. Smell signals also travel into brain areas linked to memory and emotion, so a single familiar smell can suddenly bring back a strong memory from the past.

keyWords.definition: related to the sense of smell
keyWords.example: Doctors tested the patient's olfactory nerve after the accident.

keyWords.definition: a rounded part shaped like a bulb; in the brain, the area that first processes smell signals
keyWords.example: The olfactory bulb sits just above the nasal passages.

keyWords.definition: to bring a feeling, memory, or image suddenly to mind
keyWords.example: The old photograph evoked memories of her childhood home.

keyWords.definition: designed or developed to do one particular job very well
keyWords.example: Specialized cells in the eye respond only to certain colors of light.

keyWords.definition: the lowest amount of something needed before it can be noticed or detected
keyWords.example: The sound was below the threshold most people could hear.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?
options: The tongue detects far more distinct smells than the nose does.
Colds permanently damage the olfactory bulb forever.
Flavor depends only on how food is prepared, never on biology.
Specialized receptors detect molecules, shaping both flavor and memory.
questions.why: The article traces how specialized receptors detect molecules, how signals reach the olfactory bulb, how smell and taste combine into flavor, and how smell connects strongly to memory and emotion.

wrong.A: The article says the opposite: the nose detects far more distinct smells than the tongue detects tastes.
wrong.B: The article says a cold temporarily blocks smell, not that it permanently damages the bulb.
wrong.C: The article presents flavor as a biological process, not purely a result of preparation.

questions.stem: According to the article, what structure first sorts and strengthens signals from smell receptors?
options: The olfactory epithelium
The tongue's taste buds
The olfactory bulb
The nasal cavity itself
questions.why: The article states that the olfactory bulb sorts, strengthens, and combines incoming signals before relaying them deeper into the brain.

wrong.A: The olfactory epithelium is where receptors are located, not where signals are sorted.
wrong.B: Taste buds handle taste, not smell signals.
wrong.D: The nasal cavity is the space inside the nose, not a brain structure.

questions.stem: Based on the article, about how many basic tastes can the tongue detect on its own?
options: Thousands of distinct basic tastes
A small handful, like sweet and sour
Exactly two basic tastes only
None without help from the eyes
questions.why: The article states the tongue alone can only detect a small handful of basic tastes, naming sweet, salty, sour, bitter, and umami.

wrong.A: Thousands of distinct smells are attributed to the nose, not basic tastes to the tongue.
wrong.C: The article lists five basic tastes, not two.
wrong.D: The article does not mention the eyes in relation to taste.

questions.stem: In the article, a familiar smell is said to evoke a vivid memory. What does evoke mean here?
options: To suddenly bring something to mind
To erase something completely
To combine two different smells
To block a receptor permanently
questions.why: The article describes a smell suddenly bringing back a memory, which is what evoke means here.

wrong.B: Evoking brings a memory back rather than erasing it.
wrong.C: Combining smells is a separate idea about flavor, not about evoking memory.
wrong.D: Blocking a receptor is unrelated to the meaning of evoke.

questions.stem: How does the author organize the explanation after introducing the olfactory epithelium and its receptors?
options: By listing historical dates when smell was studied
By comparing noses of several animal species
By telling a long story about one person's life
By tracing the signal's path and then its effects
questions.why: The article follows the smell signal from the receptors, through the olfactory nerve and bulb, and then explains its effects on flavor and on memory and emotion.

wrong.A: No historical dates or timeline of discovery are given.
wrong.B: The article does not compare different animal species.
wrong.C: The article is not a personal narrative about one individual.

questions.stem: According to the article, what is the direct effect of a matching molecule fitting a receptor?
options: The molecule disappears from the air instantly
The receptor fires a signal carrying information about it
The tongue begins tasting the molecule directly
The olfactory bulb shrinks slightly in size
questions.why: The article says that when a matching molecule fits snugly, the receptor fires an electrical signal carrying information about it.

wrong.A: The molecule dissolves onto moist tissue, but it is not described as disappearing instantly from the air.
wrong.C: The tongue does not taste smell molecules directly.
wrong.D: The article never mentions the bulb shrinking.

questions.stem: Which conclusion is best supported by the article's description of smell and emotion?
options: Smell is processed exactly like every other sense
Only unpleasant smells can bring back memories
Smell has an unusually direct link to memory and emotion
Memory and emotion are separate from smell entirely
questions.why: The article states smell signals travel more directly into memory and emotion areas than signals from most other senses.

wrong.A: The article specifically contrasts smell with most other senses in this regard.
wrong.B: The article does not limit this effect to unpleasant smells.
wrong.D: The article closely links smell to both memory and emotion.

questions.stem: A chef claims food tastes rich even with a blocked nose. What would the article most likely say?
options: This is unlikely, since most flavor comes from smell
This is accurate, since the tongue provides full flavor
This claim cannot be tested in any way at all
This is true only for certain sour or bitter foods
questions.why: Since the article explains that most of what people call flavor comes from smell, blocking the nose should leave food tasting dull, contradicting the chef's claim.

wrong.B: The article says the tongue detects only a few basic tastes, not full flavor.
wrong.C: The article describes exactly how a cold tests this situation.
wrong.D: The article does not single out sour or bitter foods for this effect.

HIGH.prompt: Explain the path a smell signal takes from the nose to the brain, and discuss why smell is unusually connected to memory and emotion. Use specific evidence from the article.
checklist: I traced the signal from receptors through the olfactory nerve and bulb.
I explained the link between smell and memory or emotion, using evidence from the article.
I connected ideas with transition words such as therefore, as a result, or because.
HIGH.modelAnswer: A smell begins when floating molecules reach specialized receptors in the olfactory epithelium, and a matching molecule causes a receptor to fire an electrical signal once the smell crosses a certain threshold of strength. This signal travels along the olfactory nerve to the olfactory bulb, which sorts and strengthens signals from thousands of receptors before passing a combined pattern deeper into the brain. Because this pathway connects more directly to brain areas tied to memory and emotion than most other senses do, a single familiar smell can evoke a powerful memory almost instantly, as a result of this close biological connection.
